extracted.intended_audience: aspiring artists, poets, public speakers, and general literary readers
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive reflections on what makes effective poetry, national literature, visual art inspiration, and oratory — arguing for rootedness in action, authenticity, and moral/psychological depth rather than mere polish or formal tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should spring from grand actions and virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is the school of all grand actions and grand virtues, of heroism, of the death of patriots and martyrs--of all the mighty deeds written in the pages of history--deeds of daring, and enthusiasm, devotion, and fortitude."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists should not limit study to the works of old masters; instead they should draw fuel from history's great deeds and virtues (examples given: Washington, Lawrence, Mary Stuart, Kossuth, Mazzini). Whitman argues the highest artistic impulse is kindled by moral heroism and great actions, which provide a richer 'school' for the artist than mere imitation of finished artworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the artist in every person
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is a beautiful truth that all men contain something of the artist in them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great artists may live and die ignorant of their gift; the teacher/artist should look for and cultivate latent artistical impulse in ordinary people rather than assuming it is the province of a few trained elites. The palace metaphor (a magnificent but unused palace owned by its owner) illustrates dormant potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: National literature must be rooted in popular life and nationality
rubrics_metrics.description: "So long as such literature is no born branch and offshoot of the Nationality, rooted and grown from its roots, and fibred with its fibre, it can never answer any deep call or perennial need."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To understand or create a true 'New World' literature, artists should ground work in the practical life, instincts, and transactions of the people (not only elite coteries). Whitman warns that visitors who study only social elites or polished circles miss the 'voiceless purpose' of a people; authentic literature emerges from the masses and national processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's primary office is psychological/religious development, not mere aesthetic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: "All the poems of Orientalism, with the Old and New Testaments at the centre, tend to deep and wide ... psychological development--with little, or nothing at all, of the mere esthetic, the principal verse-requirement of our day."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should pursue deep human/emotional, spiritual, and communal themes (God, Providence, covenant, nature revealed) rather than prioritizing surface beauty. Whitman highlights the Bible and oriental epics as models where religious and psychological depth outweigh formal prettiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form (rhyme and rigid metre) is not essential to poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: "Rhyming was not a characteristic of Hebrew poetry at all. Metre was not a necessary mark of poetry. Great poets discarded it; the early Jewish poets knew it not."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal devices like rhyme and strict metre are neither necessary nor definitive of great poetry; substance, metaphor, and spirit matter more. Whitman points to Hebrew and early Jewish practice as evidence that poetry's power lies beyond conventional formal constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poems must be products of real transactions and historical processes
rubrics_metrics.description: "Before there can be recorded history or poem there must be the transaction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True literature arises from real events, social processes, and national 'gestations' — not from abstract polish or sentimentalism. Whitman uses the foundry/metaphor of America�s ongoing massive processes to insist that poetry should grow out of lived, collective experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratory must convey 'action' and live feeling rather than polished elocution
rubrics_metrics.description: "The 'action, action, action,' first in its inward and then (very moderate and restrain'd) its outward sense, was the quality that had leading fulfilment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective public speaking seizes the audience by authentic, inwardly generated emotion and moral force. Whitman praises Father Taylor's extemporaneous, passionate preaching (no manuscript, strong biblical/allusive language) that probed conscience and moved listeners, contrasting this with mere trained elocution or polished rhetorical performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and unsophisticated speech often outdo trained rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: "Why is it that the unsophisticated practices often strike deeper than the train'd ones?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman observes that minor, unschooled speakers (examples: John P. Hale, Cassius Clay, abolition fanatics) sometimes have more 'life-eloquence' and effect than celebrated orators (Webster, Clay, Everett). The criterion: sincerity, immediacy, and moral urgency can be more persuasive than technical finish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend individuality with universality in great poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: "The culminated proof of the poetry of a country is the quality of its personnel...The finest blending of individuality with universality ... typified in the songs of those old Asiatic lands."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great poems/poets combine distinct, powerful individual character with universal human resonance (Whitman compares this ideal to Homer and Shakespeare). Writers should aim for works that are particular yet speak to wide human concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the Bible's enduring poetic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: "No true bard will ever contravene the Bible. If the time ever comes when iconoclasm does its extremest ... the collection must still survive ... through its divine and primal poetic structure."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman asserts the Bible's poetic forms and associative depth form an essential backbone of poetic tradition; even radical criticism cannot erase its influence. Poets should recognize and learn from this primal, communal poetic heritage.
